correctness.rationale: There are t+1 full-alphabet blocks, so every length-(t+1) target embeds and any constant length-(t+2) target fails. Greedy matching within I_q uses a new copy exactly at weak descents. If any of the first t comparisons is a strict increase, the first t+1 symbols fit in I_q^t and the last fits in π. If all are weak descents, the first t+1 cannot fit in I_q^t, so any embedding must use π for at least its last two letters. They fit exactly when their π-positions increase, and then placing the first t targets one per I_q copy suffices. For pivot v the first t symbols have binomial(q−v+t,t) choices by multisets and the last symbol has p_π(v) choices, with the q=1 case also covered. An independent distinct-subsequence-set check covered all 99 hosts with q≤4, t≤3 (34,477 length-(t+2) candidates). A separate exact subset-state dynamic program reproduced every endpoint, omission and support size for t=2, q≤7, including the cutoff among q≥3; no inference from a partial sweep was needed.
residual_risks: The analytic characterization is all-q,t; the tested and credited finite spectrum has t=2 and q≤7. No independent formal verification is claimed.

evidence: Kosche et al. give a one-position-per-arch description of SAS, and a weak-descent description for powers of one increasing permutation.
The separate one-switch record gives a two-pivot-order test and binomial product count for P^a Q^b, plus extrema and growth laws.
Adamson et al. give bounds for absent subsequences at fixed length and arch count, not the exact permutation-score support.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Taking P=I_q, Q=π, a=t, b=1 in the one-switch record gives exactly the frozen criterion and score for q≥2. This is demonstrable overlap independently of the later catalogue date. Neither the broader formula nor its optimizers give the pattern of holes at t=2.

evidence: For permutation arches the witness inequalities in the general theorem read as weak descents in the order of each corresponding arch. In the last arch the order is that of π; binomial pivot summation then yields the frozen formula.
The one-switch formula specializes to that same pivot sum. The stronger result is separately dated November 2; that timing is not treated as evidence of earlier priority.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The characterization and formula are not independent grounds for accepting novelty against the arch theory and exact overlapping formula. The t=2 support question is a separate all-permutations realizability problem absent from the inspected implications.

evidence: At t=1, the count is binomial(q+2,3) plus half the sum of squared rank displacements; §3.4.1 gives its possible values (the q=3 exception included).
At t=2 the weights are consecutive triangular numbers, not affine ranks. Neither that rank-displacement law nor the aligned permutation example determines its attainable values.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The t=1 case is exactly the classical support law after translation and scaling and is excluded. For t=2 the support is the dot product of permuted consecutive ranks with fixed triangular weights, a nonlinear weighting not obtained by this translation or scaling.

originality.rationale: Credit the exact nonlinear t=2 attainable supports and the first endpoint-only gap transition, not the general arch method, the aligned case, or the t=1 support. The two-order criterion and count can be recovered by specializing a prior general SAS characterization and counting pivot choices. A separate Resultary record also gives a directly specializing formula and extrema, but not the exact attainable supports or transition. Those require deciding which intermediate scores are realizable across permutations, not merely evaluating any one score.
residual_risks: The bounded comparison does not exclude an equivalent table or range theorem indexed under triangular-weight permutation sums. It does establish meaningful overlap in the SAS characterization and formula, which are not credited as the decisive original component.

value.rationale: The first nonlinear weighting of a natural order-dependent SAS count asks whether the extremal interval is actually filled. The two immediate endpoint gaps are intrinsic: sorting any nonextremal rank assignment toward its extremum by adjacent swaps gains at least two, the smallest difference between triangular weights. Thus q=6 is the first case among q≥3 attaining every value not ruled out by the immediate endpoint obstruction, with q=7 a second exact instance. This is a meaningful finite cutoff and gives exact data for broader support questions, not just a list at arbitrary sizes.
residual_risks: The frozen scope ends at q=7; no larger-alphabet classification is needed or credited as part of the record.
